summary: Defines a 16-bit encoding for identifying differentiated services Per Hop Behaviors in protocol messages. It replaces RFC 2836.

plainLanguage.summary: It gives each way of handling traffic a short number tag so machines can talk about it.

questions: what is a phb identification code
how is a phb encoded in 16 bits
what is a phb scheduling class
how are class selector codepoints signalled
subtitle: A 16-bit code that names a Differentiated Services Per Hop Behavior, or a set of them, inside protocol messages.

tldr.problem: Packets carry only a DSCP, and there are just 64 DSCP values while the number of Per Hop Behaviors (PHBs) is not limited. Signalling messages between domains need an unambiguous way to name a PHB or a set of PHBs.
tldr.mechanism: A PHB or set of PHBs is encoded in an unsigned 16-bit field. Standardized PHBs use their recommended DSCP, left-justified; other PHBs use a 12-bit code assigned by IANA with bit 15 set to 1. Bit 14 marks a set of PHBs.
tldr.outcome: This encoding MUST be used whenever a protocol message needs to identify a PHB. RFC 3140 replaces RFC 2836 by adding the Class Selector codepoints and a rule for PHB Scheduling Classes.

today: RFC 3140 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2001. It obsoletes RFC 2836, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why PHBs Need Identification Codes
sections.content:
In Differentiated Services, a Per Hop Behavior (PHB) defines how traffic belonging to a behavior aggregate is treated at one network node. Packet headers do not name a PHB. They carry a Differentiated Services Codepoint (DSCP) instead, and there are only 64 possible DSCP values.

There is no such limit on the number of PHBs. Within a network domain a locally defined mapping connects DSCPs to PHBs. Standardized PHBs recommend a DSCP, but operators may choose another mapping, so a bare DSCP is not a reliable name for a PHB when it crosses domains.

RFC 3140 defines a binary encoding that uniquely identifies PHBs and sets of PHBs in protocol messages. The encoding MUST be used whenever such identification is required.
sections.plainLanguage: Lots of traffic types exist but only a few labels fit on a packet. So when two networks talk about traffic types, they need a bigger, clearer name tag.

sections.title: Where the Codes Are Used
sections.content:
The RFC gives two situations. First, messages that negotiate bandwidth management or path selection, especially between management domains. Examples where work was in progress include communication between bandwidth brokers and MPLS support of diffserv.

Second, some link layers such as ATM and MPLS use connections whose forwarding behavior is a property of the connection. Different behavior aggregates can be carried on different connections. When connections are set up dynamically, the PHB, or set of PHBs, can be included in the connection establishment signalling. The ATM Forum was defining a new call setup information element to carry PHB identification codes.

Sometimes what must be named is a set of PHBs, for example the three PHBs of one Assured Forwarding class (AF11, AF12 and AF13), which must follow the same physical path to prevent re-ordering.
sections.plainLanguage: When a road has separate lanes for fast and slow traffic, the sign at the entrance has to say which lane you are in. These codes are that sign.

sections.title: The 16-Bit Encoding
sections.content:
A PHB or set of PHBs is encoded in an unsigned 16-bit binary field. There are two cases.

Case 1 covers PHBs defined by standards action. A single PHB is encoded as its recommended DSCP value, left-justified in the field, with bits 6 through 15 set to zero. The recommended DSCP MUST be used even if the local network maps the PHB to a different DSCP. A set of PHBs is encoded as the numerically smallest encoding in the set, with bit 14 set to 1. For the AF1x PHBs that is the AF11 encoding with bit 14 set.

Case 2 covers PHBs not defined by standards action, meaning experimental or local use PHBs. An arbitrary 12-bit PHB identification code, assigned by IANA, is placed left-justified in the field. Bit 15 is set to 1, bit 14 is zero for a single PHB or 1 for a set, and bits 12 and 13 are zero. Bits 12 and 13 are reserved for expansion of the code or other future use.
sections.plainLanguage: The tag is 16 little switches. For well-known traffic types, the first few switches spell the standard label. For homemade types, you get a number from the registry, and one switch says it is homemade.

sections.title: Sets Must Be Scheduling Classes
sections.content:
In both cases, when one PHBID identifies a set of PHBs (bit 14 is 1), that set MUST constitute a PHB Scheduling Class. That means using different PHBs from the set MUST NOT cause intra-microflow traffic reordering when they are applied to traffic in the same microflow.

The AF1x PHBs are the example given. Sets of PHBs that do not form a PHB Scheduling Class can still be identified, by using more than one PHBID.
sections.plainLanguage: You can only group treatments together if packets from one conversation will not get shuffled out of order by switching between them.

sections.title: Signalling the Class Selector Codepoints
sections.content:
RFC 2474 defines the eight codepoints of the form xxx000 as the Class Selector Codepoints. Codepoint 000000 is the recommended DSCP for the Default PHB, so the Case 1 PHBID built from it signals the Default PHB.

For consistency with networks that use IP Precedence, the Case 1 PHBIDs built from the other seven Class Selector Codepoints may also be used to signal PHBs. The PHB signalled is the one to which that class selector codepoint, or the corresponding IP Precedence value in non-diffserv domains, is mapped in the recipient's network. Different networks use different mappings.

Any specified use of PHBIDs SHOULD allow the eight Case 1 PHBIDs constructed from the Class Selector Codepoints.
sections.plainLanguage: Some older networks use a simple priority number. These codes let those numbers be used too, and each network decides what treatment its own number means.

sections.title: The IANA Registry
sections.content:
IANA is asked to create a registry of "Per-Hop Behavior Identification Codes", initially allowing values from 0 to 4095. An assignment requires the identity of the assignee, a brief description of the new PHB detailed enough to distinguish it from existing ones (covering every PHB in a set), and a reference to a stable document describing the PHB.

During the first year, IANA was asked to refer all requests to the IETF diffserv working group. After that, requests should be reviewed by the IETF Transport Area Directors or an expert they designate. If assignments approach 4096, the Transport Area Directors should be alerted.
sections.plainLanguage: There is an official list of homemade tags. To get one you say who you are, describe the treatment, and point to a document, so nobody gets the same tag twice.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The encoding in itself raises no security issues. However, modifying a PHB identification code may constitute theft or denial of service, so protocols that use it must be adequately protected.

Just signalling a PHBID SHOULD NOT be enough to give the sender access to a PHB it could not otherwise use. Where that matters, receivers SHOULD treat received PHBIDs as requests for service and use local policy to decide whether to grant them.
sections.plainLanguage: Asking for the express lane should not automatically get you the express lane. The receiver checks its rules first.
